excerpt: Give your agents their own computers with Cua Spaces. Watch them work, step in when you want, and share with your team.
It works in the background, so you can keep using your mouse and keyboard while the agent works. The agent gets its own cursor, so you can see what it is doing.
It works with agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. You install it once, add it to your agent, and then ask the agent to do things in your apps.
Cua Driver: lets an agent drive native apps on macOS, Windows and Linux in the background, through MCP or a CLI.
Your agent builds and tests a Windows app in the background while you keep working.
Control what the agent may do — Set permissions
Cua SDKCreate and drive computers from your own code. Python, TypeScript and Rust.
the SDK uses Docker or Podman (gVisor when installed), QEMU, or Lume on Apple silicon. Any OCI image works.
Any machine that runs cua-spacesd, such as a spare Mac, a server on your LAN or Tailscale... connects directly by address and env token.
`cua runtime doctor` shows what this host has and `cua runtime setup` installs what is missing
streams everything back so your users can watch, take over or teleport work in and out.
Start from a taskset in the Cua Bench registry: one command runs it on this machine.
`@evaluate_task` Inspects the final state and returns rewards. It scores an oracle, a human or an agent the same way.
Adapter benchmarks: OSWorld-Verified, MiniWoB++, WebVoyager and other adapters.
Lume: macOS and Linux VMs on Apple silicon.
Move a signed-in app, such as Chrome or Slack, into a Space and it opens there still signed in.
Nothing is read until you approve, and sensitive items need Touch ID. The Space checks the bundle's SHA-256 before it opens the app.
Every item is locked until you allow unattended access. Approve requests, lock or delete items, let an agent sign in to a site with a saved password
you and every agent get a cursor of your own on the same desktop. Step in whenever you want to make a call yourself, like choosing the seat, then hand it back.
Share a Space with a teammate as a viewer or an editor.
Connect a Mac on your desk, a spare box in the office or a VM in your own AWS, Google Cloud or Modal account. Each one runs Spaces
Connect another Mac, Windows or Linux computer you own to Cua Spaces... Also how to turn a spare Mac into a place that runs Spaces.
Admins set roles and approve each new device before it can reach a team computer.
Start Claude Code, Codex and other coding agents inside a Space or sandbox, and follow their work from your own agent, the CLI or code.
A named agent whose memory outlives its runs and its Space: a home in the Cua Volume, routines the daemon fires, notifications, pause and resume
One versioned drive per account, shared by every Space and agent: agent memory and outputs that outlive any Space... and an audit log.
Stream a Space desktop or one window with audio: open a media ticket, pick a codec and transport
a hotkey opens a zoomable canvas of live windows from macOS, Linux and Omarchy Spaces, with agent and coworker cursors and agent threads.
the end-to-end encrypted connections (on by default) that keep the relay from reading a session.
Remove Cua Spaces, the cua CLI and everything they set up with one command. Your Spaces and their data stay unless you ask for them to go.
No account needed to start.

User tried Cua three times. The first time it opened a macOS VM but got ahead of itself and typed in the wrong place, leaving a Finder file named "plt.ylabel('Price(USD)').sh". The next two runs launched the VM but couldn't connect to the Computer API Server WebSocket after 60s (Gradio UI, OMNI loop, gemma3:4b, cua-agent 0.1.29).
Would love to use this for TestDriver, but it needs to support Windows.
This is exactly what I'm looking for, but for Windows. We need to automate some Windows native apps. In the meantime I'll try it on macOS.

At NonBioS.ai we built something like this from scratch for Linux VMs, and it was a heavy lift. We could have used Cua if we'd known about it. I can see it being immediately useful in a lot of places.
Asked for a one-shot VM mode: an ephemeral VM spins up, the agent runs its task, and the VM is deleted. That would be perfect for CI pipelines.
Was thinking of building something like this myself and wanted a Docker alternative to e2b, so Cua fits that need.

Has used Cua's Lume CLI for about five days to sandbox Claude on a Mac and says it's been reasonably good. The only hurdle: expanding the VM's disk didn't propagate to the guest, so they had to back up and create a new VM.
Interesting project, but the lack of any actual benchmark results on existing models/agents in Cua-Bench is disappointing.
Praised Cua-Bench's trajectory export as smart: evaluation and training data collection in the same tool. Asked how it handles non-determinism like loading states, animations and intermittent popups.
